blocks.text: 1. Sampling

blocks.alt: A probability distribution goes through sampling to produce one token

blocks.text: A language model, already covered generally in Transformers, produces a probability distribution over its vocabulary at every generation step. Sampling, the process of turning that distribution into one actual chosen token, is what happens next.
It is genuinely the final step standing between raw model output and real generated text, a step explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Recapping The Probability Distribution
This connects back to the softmax function, already covered generally in Attention Mechanism. At every single generation step, the model genuinely outputs one probability for every vocabulary word.
Sampling genuinely decides which single word actually gets picked from that entire distribution, the exact mechanism explored throughout the rest of this topic.
3. Greedy Decoding

blocks.alt: A probability distribution always picks the highest token

blocks.text: This connects back to the probability distribution, already covered in this topic. The genuinely simplest strategy always picks the single highest probability word at every step.

This is genuinely deterministic and repeatable, but it genuinely produces the exact same output every single time given the exact same starting input, a genuinely real limitation explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Behavior"],"rows":[["Greedy decoding","Always picks the highest probability word, fully deterministic"],["Random sampling","Picks a word according to its own probability weight, genuinely varied"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Random Sampling From The Distribution

blocks.alt: A probability distribution gets a random draw to produce a token

blocks.text: This connects back to greedy decoding, already covered in this topic. An alternative genuinely draws a random word according to its own probability weight rather than always taking the single top word.

Higher probability words genuinely get picked more often, but lower probability words genuinely still have a real chance, a genuinely important source of variety explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Why Determinism Is Not Enough

blocks.alt: Greedy decoding produces repetitive, bland text

blocks.text: This connects back to greedy decoding always producing the exact same output, already covered in this topic. Real writing and conversation genuinely benefit from some amount of variety.
Pure determinism genuinely feels repetitive and predictable across many separate generations, a genuinely real limitation that motivates random sampling, already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This tension, already covered in this topic, directly explains why almost no production system relies on pure greedy decoding alone for open-ended generation tasks.

blocks.text: 6. Randomness Versus Quality Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Too much randomness is compared against too little randomness

blocks.text: This connects back to random sampling from the distribution, already covered in this topic. Genuinely too much randomness lets very low probability, nonsensical words slip through into the generated text.
Genuinely too little randomness collapses back toward greedy decoding's own repetitive behavior, already covered earlier in this topic, losing the variety that motivated sampling in the first place.
7. Preview Of Truncation Strategies
This connects back to the randomness versus quality tradeoff, already covered in this topic. Genuinely practical sampling strategies truncate the distribution before sampling from it.

Temperature, top-k sampling, and top-p sampling, covered as separate later topics in this module, are exactly these truncation strategies, each genuinely managing that same tradeoff in its own distinct way.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This preview, already covered in this topic, sets up temperature, top-k sampling, and top-p sampling as later, more detailed topics in this same module, each building directly on the general sampling idea covered here.

blocks.text: 8. The Autoregressive Generation Loop

blocks.alt: A sampled token is appended to the sequence, then the loop repeats

blocks.text: This connects back to sampling picking one token, already covered in this topic. That genuinely chosen token then genuinely feeds back in as part of the input for the very next step.
Sampling genuinely repeats at every single step until an entire sequence has been generated, a genuinely repeated loop explored throughout the rest of this topic's own worked example.
9. Recognizing When Each Sampling Style Is Genuinely Appropriate

blocks.alt: Needing creative, varied output points toward random sampling

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely needing reproducible, deterministic output, already covered in this topic. Greedy decoding, already covered in this topic, directly delivers exactly that reproducibility.
This connects back to genuinely wanting varied, creative output instead, already covered in this topic. Random sampling, already covered, remains the genuinely better choice for that variety.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sampling turns a language model's probability distribution over its vocabulary into one chosen token.
Greedy decoding always picks the single highest probability word, fully deterministic but repetitive.
Random sampling draws a word weighted by its own probability, adding genuine variety.
Pure determinism feels repetitive across many generations, motivating the case for sampling.
Too much randomness lets nonsensical words through; too little collapses back toward greedy decoding.
Temperature, top-k sampling, and top-p sampling are practical strategies that truncate the distribution first.
The chosen token at each step feeds back in as input for the next step, repeating the sampling process.
Greedy decoding suits reproducibility; random sampling suits varied, creative generation.
Next up: Temperature, the first of the truncation strategies previewed in this topic.
